title: Sorrow into joy (John 16:20–22)
hook: like a woman in labor, whose sorrow turns to joy
carry: your joy no man shall take
tomorrow: That they all may be one

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Spirit of truth, who leads into what we can't yet carry. Your line was not yet, but coming.

Ask anyone who has given birth, or stood in a delivery room beside someone who has. The hours before are hard to describe and harder to sit through. Then, almost in the same minute, the room changes. The baby is crying, someone is laughing, someone is texting a photo to the whole family. Hours of pain, and then something that doesn't erase the pain so much as outweigh it. Jesus is still at the supper, and his friends are confused. A little while, he keeps saying, and you won't see me. To explain, he reaches for a birth.
screen: `THE HOURS BEFORE.` → `THEN THE ROOM CHANGES.` → `A LITTLE WHILE.`

segments.voice: The disciples are whispering among themselves: what does he mean, a little while? Jesus hears them and answers straight. You will weep and lament, and the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful. Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "your sorrow shall be turned into joy." It doesn't say replaced. It says turned. The same sorrow becomes the joy, the way the labor itself becomes the birth. Then the picture. A woman in labor has sorrow, because her hour has come. That word again, hour, the word John uses for the cross. But when the child is born, she doesn't remember the anguish anymore, for joy that a person has come into the world. And he finishes: "So also you now indeed have sorrow; but I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice; and your joy no man shall take from you." At Easter, they'll see him again. That's the first meaning. But the Church has read it more widely. Joy, in this picture, isn't the absence of grief. It's on the far side of it, and it isn't fragile: no one can take it. Catholics live this in the rhythm of the year: the fast of Lent, the sorrow of Good Friday, and then an Easter season that runs all the way to Pentecost. And some who have walked through a real loss describe something like it: the grief didn't go away, but it was turned, slowly, into something they wouldn't give back.
screen: `A LITTLE WHILE, AND YOU WEEP.` · `NOT REPLACED: TURNED.` · `THE WOMAN IN LABOR.` · `JOY NO ONE CAN TAKE.` · then, large: `SORROW INTO JOY.`

segments.voice: Breathe slowly and steadily, the way a birth coach counts: in for four, out for six. If you're in a painful season right now, name it quietly, without making it mean anything yet, and breathe through it one breath at a time; if you're not, hold someone who is. If you pray, hold the line, your sorrow shall be turned into joy; if you don't, just keep breathing.
Joy. Jesus's promise at the supper: grief, like labor, turned into a joy no one can take. Today's word.
Your line: your joy no man shall take. Not instead of the grief, but on the far side of it. That's day five hundred twenty-four.

fork.setup: your friends are confused and frightened. you need to explain that grief is coming, and then joy. what picture do you use?
fork.reveal: Jesus uses birth: a woman in labor has sorrow, but when the child is born she remembers the anguish no more, for joy.

trapdoor: what you thought: cheer up, it gets better.
what it means: the sorrow itself is turned, like labor into birth, into a joy no one can take away.
what a scholar hears: the woman's 'hour' (hōra) echoes John's word for the cross; birth pangs are an image the prophets use for the coming age (e.g. Isaiah 26:17–19).

chat.says: Does Jesus promise his friends they won't ever be sad?
options: No, he says they'll weep, but their sorrow will be turned into a joy no one can take.
Yes, he promises the sorrow will be wiped away and replaced, as if it never was.
No, he says joy belongs to the world, and sorrow is all his friends will have.
chat.meaning: Jesus says they will weep. Then their sorrow is turned into joy, like labor into birth, and no one can take it.
